主要内容: On October 12, 2017, President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at expanding health-coverage options and reducing costs for millions of Americans. The order directs federal agencies to consider loosening rules controlling the issuance of health coverage by groups of businesses and the duration of short-term health plans that do not currently meet Obamacare rules. While the order is not expected to have a significant impact on enrollment for the upcoming sign-up season, it could change if the administration makes other changes related to Obamacare's penalties in the coming weeks. The order does not lift the Obamacare rule that most Americans have some form of health insurance for the year or face a tax penalty. Gary Claxton of the Kaiser Family Foundation noted that the order may not accomplish much in the short-term. Trump emphasized that the order is the beginning of a series of measures to provide relief and freedom to Americans under the Affordable Care Act. The order also aims to expand access to Association Health Plans (AHPs), allowing small businesses to form groups to purchase health insurance collectively. This could lead to increased competition among insurers, as AHPs can operate across state lines. Critics argue that this could reduce the number of healthy individuals enrolling in individual plans on Obamacare exchanges, potentially leading to higher premiums. The order suggests revisiting the Obama administration's restrictions on short-term insurance plans, which currently do not meet Obamacare's coverage requirements. Some see this as offering more choice, while others warn it could create market instability by separating healthier and more complex consumers into different pools. The administration is also looking into ways to increase competition among healthcare providers and insurers, citing concerns over consolidation in the sector since the ACA's implementation.
